title: Climate, Weather and Climate Change
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Science 0893 · Stage 8 · Earth and Space
summary: The difference between weather and climate, the evidence that the Earth's climate cycles between ice ages and warm periods, and how changes in the atmosphere change the climate — with graphs, worked examples and a Checkpoint-style quiz.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Understand that there is evidence that the Earth's climate moves in a cycle between warm periods and ice ages, and that this cycle takes place over very long periods of time. (8ESc.01)
Understand that the Earth's climate can change because the atmosphere changes. (8ESc.02)
Describe the difference between climate and weather. (8ESc.03)

blocks.text: 2. Weather and climate are not the same

**Weather** is what the air is like at one place **at one time**: how hot or cold it is, whether it is raining, how strong the wind is, how cloudy it is. Weather changes from hour to hour and from day to day. A sandstorm in Cairo this afternoon is weather.

**Climate** is the **average weather** of a region over a **long time** — scientists usually use at least **30 years** of measurements. Climate tells you what to **expect**. "Egypt has hot, dry summers and mild winters with very little rain" describes Egypt's climate.

rows: Time
Short: hours, days, a week
Long: average over 30 years or more
Area
A place (a town, a city)
A larger region or the whole Earth
Changes
Changes quickly, every day
Changes slowly, over many years
Example sentence
"It will rain in Alexandria tomorrow afternoon."
"Alexandria has warm, dry summers and mild, wet winters."
Words to spot
today, tomorrow, this week, at the moment, yesterday
usually, on average, every year, typical, over 30 years

blocks.title: A sentence to remember
blocks.text: **Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get.** You expect a hot summer in Luxor (climate), but one particular day might be cloudy (weather).
Scientists show a climate with a **climate graph**: bars for the average rainfall in each month and a line for the average temperature.

blocks.title: الطقس ولا المناخ؟
blocks.text: **الطقس** = حالة الجو **النهارده** أو **الأسبوع ده** في مكان معين (مطر، رياح، حرارة) وبيتغير بسرعة. **المناخ** = **متوسط** الطقس في منطقة على مدى **سنين كتير** (حوالي ٣٠ سنة أو أكتر). لو الجملة فيها "النهارده / بكره / امبارح" يبقى **طقس**؛ لو فيها "عادةً / في المتوسط / كل سنة" يبقى **مناخ**.
3. The Earth's climate moves in a cycle

The Earth's climate has never stayed the same. For hundreds of thousands of years it has moved in a **cycle**: long, cold **ice ages**, when huge ice sheets covered much of North America and northern Europe, and shorter **warm periods** between them. We are living in a warm period now; it began about 11 700 years ago.

items: One full cycle (from one warm period to the next) takes about **100 000 years** — far longer than human history.
The temperature usually **falls slowly** into an ice age over tens of thousands of years, then **rises quite quickly** into a warm period.
At the coldest point of the last ice age, about 20 000 years ago, so much water was frozen in ice sheets that the sea level was about 120 m lower than today.
Scientists think the cycle is started by slow changes in the Earth's path around the Sun and in the tilt of its axis. These change how much sunlight reaches different parts of the Earth.

blocks.text: 4. The evidence for ice ages and warm periods
Nobody was measuring temperatures 100 000 years ago, so how do we know? Scientists use several kinds of **evidence**, and they all agree with each other.

rows: **Ice cores**
Long cylinders of ice drilled from Antarctica and Greenland. Snow falls in layers each year and becomes ice, trapping **tiny bubbles of air**. The Antarctic cores go back about 800 000 years.
The deeper the ice, the older it is. The air bubbles show how much carbon dioxide was in the air then, and the ice itself shows how cold it was. Both rise and fall in the same cycle.
**Fossils**
Fossils of animals and plants that need a warm climate (e.g. hippopotamus bones in Britain) and of cold-climate animals (e.g. woolly mammoths) in places where they could not live today
The climate of that place was once warmer, or colder, than now
**Rocks and landscapes**
U-shaped valleys and huge boulders carried hundreds of kilometres from where they formed, in places with no ice today
Glaciers and ice sheets once covered these areas
**Sediments and pollen**
Layers of mud at the bottom of oceans and lakes, with shells of tiny sea creatures and pollen grains
Which plants grew and how warm the sea was, layer by layer, over time

blocks.text: 5. Climate can change when the atmosphere changes
The **atmosphere** is the layer of gases around the Earth. Some of these gases — **carbon dioxide**, **methane** and **water vapour** — are **greenhouse gases**. This is how they warm the Earth:

items: Energy from the Sun (sunlight) passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface.
The warm surface gives off energy as **heat** (infrared).
Some heat escapes to space, but greenhouse gases **absorb** some of it and send it back towards the Earth.
So the atmosphere **traps heat**, like the glass of a greenhouse — this is the **greenhouse effect**.

blocks.text: The greenhouse effect is natural and we need it: without it the Earth's average temperature would be about −18 °C, too cold for most life. The problem is when the amount of greenhouse gas **increases** — more heat is trapped and the climate warms.

rows: **More carbon dioxide**
Burning **fossil fuels** (coal, oil, natural gas) in power stations, cars and factories; **deforestation** (fewer trees take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, and burning forests releases it)
More heat trapped → **warming**
**More methane**
Cattle and other farm animals, rice fields, rubbish in landfill sites, leaks from natural gas
More heat trapped → **warming**
**Volcanic ash and gases** high in the atmosphere
A very large volcanic eruption
Blocks some sunlight → **cooling** for a year or two
Carbon dioxide rising and falling naturally
Part of the ice-age cycle (the ice cores show less carbon dioxide during ice ages)
Makes the natural warming and cooling stronger

blocks.text: **The evidence today:** careful measurements since 1958 show that the carbon dioxide in the air has risen every year, from about 317 parts per million in 1960 to more than 410 in 2020. Ice cores show it was never above about 300 parts per million in the 800 000 years before the Industrial Revolution. Over the same time the Earth's average temperature has risen by more than 1 °C. Most scientists agree that this change is caused mainly by humans burning fossil fuels.

**Possible effects of climate change:** sea levels rise (ice on land melts and sea water expands when it warms) — a danger for low coasts such as the Nile Delta; more heatwaves, droughts and floods; habitats change and some species cannot survive (for example coral reefs in the Red Sea can be damaged by hot water). We can reduce the change by using **renewable** energy, saving energy, and planting trees.

blocks.title: القاعدة الأساسية
blocks.text: غازات الدفيئة (زي **ثاني أكسيد الكربون** و**الميثان**) بتحبس الحرارة في الغلاف الجوي. لما نحرق **الوقود الأحفوري** بيزيد ثاني أكسيد الكربون ← حرارة أكتر بتتحبس ← **الأرض بتسخن**. يعني **تغيّر الغلاف الجوي = تغيّر المناخ**.
6. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Tick (✓) to show whether each sentence describes **weather** or **climate**. [3]

rows: (a) It is raining heavily in Alexandria this morning.
(b) Cairo has hot, dry summers and mild winters.
(c) Tomorrow will be windy, with a highest temperature of 31 °C.
(d) Aswan gets very little rain in a typical year.
(e) Yesterday there was a sandstorm.

items: Look for time words: "this morning", "tomorrow", "yesterday" → **weather** (a, c, e).
"Has hot summers", "in a typical year" describe what is usual over many years → **climate** (b, d).
Marks: 5 correct = 3; 4 correct = 2; 3 correct = 1.
**Common mistake:** (d) is about rain, so students tick weather. Rain can be part of climate — the key words are **typical year**.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — Use the climate graph in section 2. (a) Which is the wettest month? [1] (b) Calculate the range of average temperature. [1] (c) Describe the climate of the city. [2] (d) Explain why this is a climate graph and not a weather record. [1]

items: (a) **December** (55 mm, the tallest bar).
(b) Highest 28 °C (August) − lowest 14 °C (January) = **14 °C**. Include the unit.
(c) Summers are hot and dry (1); winters are mild/cool and wetter (1). Quote numbers if you can: about 28 °C and no rain in summer.
(d) The values are **averages over 30 years**, not measurements from one day or one year (1).

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — Use the ice-age graph in section 3. (a) Is the Earth in a warm period or an ice age now? [1] (b) About how long is one cycle from one warm period to the next? [1] (c) Describe how ice cores give evidence for this cycle. [2]

items: (a) A **warm period** (the line is at the warm level, 0 °C compared with today, at the right-hand end).
(b) The warm peaks are about 400, 335, 245 and 128 thousand years ago, roughly 100 thousand years apart → about **100 000 years**.

(c) Snow builds up in yearly layers, so deeper ice is older (1); the ice and the trapped air bubbles show the temperature and the carbon dioxide at that time, and they go up and down in a repeating pattern (1).
**Common mistake:** writing 100 years or 1000 years. The cycle is **very long** — about a hundred thousand years.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — Explain how burning fossil fuels can change the Earth's climate. [3]

items: Burning fossil fuels releases **carbon dioxide** into the atmosphere (1).
Carbon dioxide is a **greenhouse gas**; it traps heat / stops some heat escaping to space (1).
More trapped heat makes the Earth's **average temperature rise** (global warming / climate change) (1).
**Exam tip:** 3 marks = 3 linked steps: gas released → traps heat → temperature rises. Do not say the gas "makes a hole" — that is a different topic (the ozone layer).

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — In 1991 a very large volcano erupted in the Philippines. For about the next two years, the Earth's average temperature was slightly lower. Suggest why. [2]

items: The eruption threw ash and gases high into the **atmosphere** (1).
These blocked / reflected some **sunlight**, so less energy reached the Earth's surface and it cooled (1).
This shows that **any change in the atmosphere can change the climate** — warming or cooling.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Mixing up weather and climate. One cold winter, or one hot week, is **weather**. Climate is the **average over 30 years or more**.
Saying ice ages happen every few hundred years. The cycle takes about **100 000 years**.
Thinking the greenhouse effect is always bad. The natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough for life; the problem is **extra** greenhouse gas.
Writing "carbon dioxide makes a hole in the atmosphere". Carbon dioxide **traps heat**; the ozone hole is a different problem.
Saying oxygen or nitrogen are greenhouse gases. The ones to know are **carbon dioxide**, **methane** and **water vapour**.
Describing ice-core evidence without saying **why** it works: deeper ice is older, and the air bubbles are samples of old air.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Tick a table**: is each sentence weather or climate?

**Read a long-time graph** (often hundreds of thousands of years): find a warm period or ice age, read a temperature, work out roughly how long a cycle takes. Check the axis — the time is often in **thousands of years**.
**Describe evidence** for ice ages (ice cores, fossils, rocks) — say what is found **and** what it shows.
**Explain** how a change in the atmosphere changes the climate — use the chain: gas → traps heat → temperature rises.
**Link two graphs** — e.g. carbon dioxide and temperature rising and falling together in ice-core data.
**Evaluate a claim** such as "It was cold last week, so the climate is not warming" — answer with the weather/climate difference.

questions.e: Climate averages are usually worked out from **30 years** (or more) of measurements.

questions.q: (c) About how long does one cycle take, from one warm period to the next?
questions.e: The warm peaks are about 400, 335, 245 and 128 thousand years ago — roughly **100 000 years** apart. Remember that the time axis is in **thousands** of years.

questions.q: Name the greenhouse gas that is released when fossil fuels are burned.
questions.e: Burning coal, oil and natural gas releases **carbon dioxide** (CO₂), a greenhouse gas.

questions.q: Which of these is evidence that the Earth has had ice ages in the past?
c: Air bubbles trapped in deep ice drilled from Antarctica
The number of hours of sunshine in Cairo this month
questions.e: **Ice cores** contain air bubbles and layers of ice up to about 800 000 years old; they show the temperature and carbon dioxide going up and down in a cycle. The other options are recent weather data.

questions.q: Which gas is a greenhouse gas?
questions.e: **Methane** (from cattle, rice fields, landfill and gas leaks) traps heat. Oxygen and nitrogen make up most of the air but are not greenhouse gases.

questions.q: By how much did the carbon dioxide increase from 1960 to 2020?
questions.e: 1960: about 317 parts per million; 2020: about 414 parts per million (1). Increase = 414 − 317 = **97 parts per million** (1) (answers from 94 to 100 accepted for careful graph reading).

questions.q: Explain how an increase in carbon dioxide in the atmosphere can lead to climate change. [3]
questions.ms: 1 mark: carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas. 1 mark: it traps heat / absorbs heat given off by the Earth / stops heat escaping to space. 1 mark: so the Earth's average temperature rises / global warming. Do not accept: 'it makes a hole in the ozone layer'. Ignore: 'pollution' without further detail.
questions.e: Carbon dioxide is a **greenhouse gas** (1). More of it **traps more heat** in the atmosphere instead of letting it escape into space (1). So the Earth's **average temperature rises**, which changes the climate (1).

questions.q: Youssef says: "Last winter was colder than usual where I live, so the Earth's climate cannot be getting warmer." Explain why Youssef's argument is weak. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: one cold winter (in one place) is weather / is a short time. 1 mark: climate is the average over a long time (about 30 years or more) / over the whole Earth, and the average can still be rising. Accept: one result is not enough evidence for a trend.
questions.e: One cold winter in one place is **weather** — a short time in a small area (1). Climate change is about the **average over many years (30 or more) across the whole Earth**, and that average can rise even if some winters are cold (1).

blocks.title: Remember
items: **Weather** = conditions at one place at one time; changes daily. **Climate** = average weather over a long time (30 years or more).
The Earth's climate moves in a **cycle** of **ice ages** and **warm periods**, about **100 000 years** long; we live in a warm period now.
Evidence: **ice cores** (layers and air bubbles), **fossils**, rocks and landscapes shaped by ice, sediments.
Greenhouse gases (**carbon dioxide**, **methane**, water vapour) **trap heat** in the atmosphere.
**A change in the atmosphere changes the climate**: more carbon dioxide (fossil fuels, deforestation) → warming; volcanic ash → short cooling.
